newsitem.title: GERMANY: German firms take Daimler line on sick pay.
newsitem.headline: German firms take Daimler line on sick pay.

text.p: A wave of German companies on Wednesday followed the lead of industrial giant Daimler-Benz AG in announcing cuts in sick pay, turning up the heat in a battle over liberalising the country's restrictive work rules.

Companies from chemical group BASF AG to bank Bayerische Vereinsbank and engineering group Mannesmann said they would implement the law beginning on October 1 that cuts sick pay to 80 percent of normal wages.
German heavyweights Hoechst AG, the chemicals and pharmaceuticals group, and electronics group Siemens AG also said they would implement the new law.

Up until now sick pay was paid at 100 percent of normal salary, worth about 60 billion marks ($40 million) in 1995. German corporate leaders have said the policy was abused on top of liberal holiday allowances.

Daimler on Tuesday took the lead in implementing the controversial legislation, linking the cutbacks to its ability to remain competitive in international markets and saying it would negotiate with unions to reduce sick pay.
A Daimler spokesman on Wednesday said the group expected to save about one percent, or hundreds of millions of marks, in wage costs due to the new plan.
But the company's works council and unions reacted with outrage. Officials said Daimler's 220,000-member workforce in Germany would refuse to work overtime and weekend shifts.

Daimler works council chairman Karl Feuerstein said talks with Daimler on trimming one billion marks ($663.5 million) a year in operating costs at Mercedes commercial vehicle plants in Germany had been broken off.

"A once noble German company is at the vanguard of breaking contracts," said Gerhard Zambelli, the leader of the powerful IG Metall union in the state of Baden-Wuerttemberg where Daimler has its headquarters.
But Daimler found support from BASF AG, which said it would also change its sick pay rules effective October 1 for its 44,000 workers in Germany.

Mannesmann AG also said it was recommending to its subsidiaries to cut sick pay. Others who said they would follow the new policy include tyre maker Continental AG, pharmaceuticals group Schering AG and Bayerische Hypo-Bank AG.

Unions and some top politicians said German companies had no right to make the sick pay cutback so quickly, arguing that the bill passed by Bonn earlier this month was not meant to apply to existing contracts but only future ones.
But Daimler and other industrial leaders have taken a sharply different view and intend to use the legislation as a way to force more flexibile working conditions.

The new policy, part of Chancellor Helmut Kohl's austerity plan to boost weak employment and whip Germany's finances into shape for European currency union, will likely lead to more labour unrest during the autumn, union leaders said.

IG Metall said it was planning protests against the new law, including a nationwide metalworkers union protest day on October 10. A week-long protest is also being planned and a day of action with all German unions.

The quick industrial changes could spell trouble for Kohl. On Tuesday the Chancellor called on employers and unions to avoid escalating the fight over sick pay and said the two sides should resolve their differences through negotiation.
At the centre of the debate is the issue of whether the government's sick pay laws are meant to apply to existing contracts or only those in the future. ($1=1.5070 Mark)
